request.user:
[2025 summer phd math-stat — problem 2]

Part III, Problem 2 (50 pts). Let $X_1, \dots, X_n$ be i.i.d. with density $p_\theta(\cdot)$; let $l_n(\theta)$ be the negative log-likelihood with Hessian $H_n(\theta)$, regularity conditions satisfied.
(i) To estimate $\psi(\theta)$, state the Cramér-Rao lower bound for any unbiased $T(X)$ with $\mathbb{E}[T(X)] = \psi(\theta)$, and prove your statement.
(ii) Given an initial estimator $\tilde\theta$ with $\|\tilde\theta - \theta\|_2 = o_p(n^{-1/4})$ and $H_n(\theta)$ $L$-Lipschitz, construct the Newton-Raphson (one-step) estimator $\hat\theta$ and show it is asymptotically normal and achieves the Cramér-Rao lower bound. (Hint: you may assume the MLE is asymptotically efficient.)

response.text:
Let the true parameter be denoted by \(\theta_0\in\Theta\subset\mathbb R^d\). Write

\[
\ell_n(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^n \log p_\theta(X_i),\qquad l_n(\theta)=-\ell_n(\theta),
\]

so that

\[
U_n(\theta)=\nabla_\theta \ell_n(\theta)=-\nabla_\theta l_n(\theta)
\]

is the score, and

\[
H_n(\theta)=\nabla_\theta^2 l_n(\theta)
\]

is the observed information. Let

\[
I(\theta)=\mathbb E_\theta\left[s_\theta(X)s_\theta(X)^\top\right],
\qquad s_\theta(x)=\nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(x),
\]

be the Fisher information for one observation. Then

\[
J_n(\theta):=\mathbb E_\theta[U_n(\theta)U_n(\theta)^\top]
=\mathbb E_\theta[H_n(\theta)]
=nI(\theta).
\]

Assume \(I(\theta)\) is nonsingular.

---

## (i) Cramér–Rao lower bound for \(\psi(\theta)\)

Let \(\psi:\Theta\to\mathbb R^k\) be differentiable, and let \(T=T(X_1,\dots,X_n)\in\mathbb R^k\) be unbiased:

\[
\mathbb E_\theta[T]=\psi(\theta).
\]

Let \(\dot\psi(\theta)\) denote the \(k\times d\) Jacobian matrix of \(\psi\). Then the Cramér–Rao lower bound is

\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(T)\ \succeq\ \dot\psi(\theta)\,J_n(\theta)^{-1}\,\dot\psi(\theta)^\top
}
\]

or, since \(J_n(\theta)=nI(\theta)\),

\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(T)\ \succeq\ \frac1n\,\dot\psi(\theta)\,I(\theta)^{-1}\,\dot\psi(\theta)^\top.
}
\]

In the scalar case \(k=1\), this becomes

\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{Var}_\theta(T)\ge \frac1n\,\nabla\psi(\theta)^\top I(\theta)^{-1}\nabla\psi(\theta).
}
\]

### Proof

Let \(f_\theta(x_1,\dots,x_n)=\prod_{i=1}^n p_\theta(x_i)\). Under the regularity conditions, differentiation under the integral sign is valid.

First,

\[
\mathbb E_\theta[U_n(\theta)]
=
\int \nabla_\theta \log f_\theta(x)\, f_\theta(x)\,dx
=
\int \nabla_\theta f_\theta(x)\,dx
=
\nabla_\theta 1
=0.
\]

Because \(T\) is unbiased,

\[
\psi(\theta)=\mathbb E_\theta[T].
\]

Differentiating,

\[
\dot\psi(\theta)
=
\nabla_\theta \mathbb E_\theta[T]
=
\int T(x)\,\nabla_\theta f_\theta(x)^\top\,dx.
\]

Since \(\nabla_\theta f_\theta=f_\theta U_n(\theta)\),

\[
\dot\psi(\theta)
=
\mathbb E_\theta[T\,U_n(\theta)^\top].
\]

Using \(\mathbb E_\theta[U_n(\theta)]=0\), this is

\[
\dot\psi(\theta)
=
\mathbb E_\theta\bigl[(T-\psi(\theta))U_n(\theta)^\top\bigr]
=
\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(T,U_n).
\]

Now consider the joint covariance matrix of \((T,U_n)\):

\[
\begin{pmatrix}
\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(T) & \dot\psi(\theta)\\
\dot\psi(\theta)^\top & J_n(\theta)
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

This matrix is positive semidefinite. Since \(J_n(\theta)\) is nonsingular, the Schur complement is also positive semidefinite:

\[
\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(T)
-
\dot\psi(\theta)J_n(\theta)^{-1}\dot\psi(\theta)^\top
\succeq 0.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(T)\succeq \dot\psi(\theta)J_n(\theta)^{-1}\dot\psi(\theta)^\top
=
\frac1n\dot\psi(\theta)I(\theta)^{-1}\dot\psi(\theta)^\top.
\]

This proves the Cramér–Rao lower bound. \(\square\)

---

## (ii) One-step Newton–Raphson estimator and efficiency

Let \(\tilde\theta\) be an initial estimator satisfying

\[
\|\tilde\theta-\theta_0\|_2=o_p(n^{-1/4}).
\]

Assume \(H_n\) is locally Lipschitz. Since \(H_n\) is the Hessian of the unnormalized negative log-likelihood, the natural condition is that \(n^{-1}H_n\) is locally \(L\)-Lipschitz, i.e.

\[
\left\|\frac1nH_n(\theta)-\frac1nH_n(\theta')\right\|
\le L\|\theta-\theta'\|
\]

with probability tending to one in a neighborhood of \(\theta_0\). Equivalently,

\[
\|H_n(\theta)-H_n(\theta')\|\le nL\|\theta-\theta'\|.
\]

The one-step Newton–Raphson estimator is

\[
\boxed{
\hat\theta
=
\tilde\theta
-
H_n(\tilde\theta)^{-1}\nabla l_n(\tilde\theta).
}
\]

Equivalently, since \(U_n=-\nabla l_n\),

\[
\hat\theta
=
\tilde\theta
+
H_n(\tilde\theta)^{-1}U_n(\tilde\theta).
\]

We show that this estimator is asymptotically equivalent to the MLE.

Let \(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}\) denote the MLE. By the hint, assume the MLE is asymptotically efficient:

\[
\sqrt n(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}-\theta_0)
\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}
N_d(0,I(\theta_0)^{-1}).
\]

In particular,

\[
\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}-\theta_0=O_p(n^{-1/2}).
\]

Define

\[
\delta_n=\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}-\tilde\theta.
\]

Then

\[
\|\delta_n\|
\le
\|\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}-\theta_0\|
+
\|\tilde\theta-\theta_0\|
=
O_p(n^{-1/2})+o_p(n^{-1/4})
=
o_p(n^{-1/4}).
\]

Because \(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}\) satisfies the likelihood equation,

\[
\nabla l_n(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}})=0.
\]

Taylor expand \(\nabla l_n\) around \(\tilde\theta\). We have

\[
0
=
\nabla l_n(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}})
=
\nabla l_n(\tilde\theta)
+
H_n(\tilde\theta)(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}-\tilde\theta)
+
r_n,
\]

where the remainder can be written as

\[
r_n
=
\int_0^1
\left[
H_n(\tilde\theta+t\delta_n)-H_n(\tilde\theta)
\right]\delta_n\,dt.
\]

Using the Lipschitz condition,

\[
\|r_n\|
\le
\int_0^1 nL\,t\,\|\delta_n\|^2\,dt
=
\frac{nL}{2}\|\delta_n\|^2.
\]

Thus

\[
\nabla l_n(\tilde\theta)
=
-H_n(\tilde\theta)\delta_n-r_n.
\]

Plugging this into the one-step estimator gives

\[
\hat\theta
=
\tilde\theta
-
H_n(\tilde\theta)^{-1}\nabla l_n(\tilde\theta)
=
\tilde\theta
+
\delta_n
+
H_n(\tilde\theta)^{-1}r_n.
\]

Since \(\tilde\theta+\delta_n=\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}\),

\[
\hat\theta-\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}
=
H_n(\tilde\theta)^{-1}r_n.
\]

By regularity,

\[
\frac1nH_n(\tilde\theta)\overset{p}{\longrightarrow} I(\theta_0),
\]

so with probability tending to one, \(H_n(\tilde\theta)\) is invertible and

\[
\|H_n(\tilde\theta)^{-1}\|=O_p(n^{-1}).
\]

Therefore,

\[
\|\hat\theta-\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}\|
\le
O_p(n^{-1})\cdot O_p(n\|\delta_n\|^2)
=
O_p(\|\delta_n\|^2).
\]

But \(\|\delta_n\|=o_p(n^{-1/4})\), so

\[
\|\delta_n\|^2=o_p(n^{-1/2}).
\]

Hence

\[
\boxed{
\hat\theta-\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}=o_p(n^{-1/2}).
}
\]

Consequently,

\[
\sqrt n(\hat\theta-\theta_0)
=
\sqrt n(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}-\theta_0)
+
\sqrt n(\hat\theta-\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}})
=
\sqrt n(\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MLE}}-\theta_0)+o_p(1).
\]

By Slutsky’s theorem,

\[
\boxed{
\sqrt n(\hat\theta-\theta_0)
\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}
N_d(0,I(\theta_0)^{-1}).
}
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\hat\theta
=
\theta_0
+
I(\theta_0)^{-1}\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n s_{\theta_0}(X_i)
+
o_p(n^{-1/2}).
\]

Thus \(\hat\theta\) has the same first-order asymptotic distribution as the MLE.

For estimating \(\psi(\theta_0)\), use the plug-in estimator \(\psi(\hat\theta)\). By the delta method,

\[
\sqrt n\left(\psi(\hat\theta)-\psi(\theta_0)\right)
\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}
N_k\left(
0,
\dot\psi(\theta_0)I(\theta_0)^{-1}\dot\psi(\theta_0)^\top
\right).
\]

Therefore the asymptotic covariance is

\[
\frac1n
\dot\psi(\theta_0)I(\theta_0)^{-1}\dot\psi(\theta_0)^\top,
\]

which is exactly the Cramér–Rao lower bound from part (i). Hence the one-step estimator is asymptotically efficient and achieves the Cramér–Rao lower bound to first order.
